questions.question: In the standard multi-armed bandit, feedback is typically a scalar reward. How does the dueling bandit setting change the feedback model?
questions.choice_A: It provides pairwise preference feedback indicating which of two chosen arms is preferred
questions.choice_B: It provides the average reward of all arms at each round
questions.choice_C: It reveals the exact latent utility values of all arms
questions.choice_D: It only provides a binary success/failure for a single arm

questions.question: Which statement best describes the goal of contextual dueling bandits?
questions.choice_A: To estimate the global preference matrix without using context
questions.choice_B: To learn a policy mapping contexts to arms that performs well under pairwise preferences
questions.choice_C: To minimize the number of contexts observed before acting
questions.choice_D: To convert pairwise feedback into absolute rewards for each arm

questions.question: What is the von Neumann winner in the context of preference-based bandits?
questions.choice_A: The arm with the highest average payoff against all others
questions.choice_B: Any arm that beats all others with probability greater than 1/2
questions.choice_C: A mixed strategy that maximizes its worst-case expected preference against the best adversarial mixture
questions.choice_D: The arm with the highest Copeland score

questions.question: Why is the von Neumann winner often preferred over the Condorcet winner in dueling bandits?
questions.choice_A: Because it requires fewer samples to identify exactly
questions.choice_B: Because a Condorcet winner may not exist due to cycles, while a von Neumann winner always exists
questions.choice_C: Because it directly maximizes cumulative reward rather than preference probabilities
questions.choice_D: Because it is equivalent to the best single arm under any noise model

questions.question: In offline preference learning for dueling bandits, which data characteristic is most critical for generalization guarantees?
questions.choice_A: The number of arms is prime
questions.choice_B: The pairwise comparisons are obtained from deterministic oracles
questions.choice_C: The coverage and diversity of compared pairs across contexts or features
questions.choice_D: The presence of at least one Condorcet winner

questions.question: Which regret notion is most aligned with the von Neumann winner in dueling bandits?
questions.choice_A: Regret relative to the best fixed arm’s expected scalar reward
questions.choice_B: Maximin regret relative to the optimal mixed strategy in the preference game
questions.choice_C: Pseudo-regret with respect to the Borda score
questions.choice_D: Contextual regret relative to the Bayes-optimal classifier

questions.question: What is a common assumption in stochastic preference models like Bradley–Terry–Luce (BTL)?
questions.choice_A: Each pair of arms is equally likely to tie
questions.choice_B: There exists a latent utility for each arm such that pairwise preference probabilities are a monotone function of utility differences
questions.choice_C: Pairwise outcomes are adversarially chosen
questions.choice_D: Preferences are transitive with probability 1

questions.question: Which algorithmic idea is characteristic of many dueling bandit algorithms like RUCB and Relative UCB?
questions.choice_A: Using point estimates of absolute rewards with upper confidence bounds
questions.choice_B: Maintaining confidence intervals over pairwise win probabilities and eliminating dominated arms
questions.choice_C: Using Thompson sampling over Gaussian reward models
questions.choice_D: Selecting the arm with the maximum empirical mean reward

questions.question: How do contextual dueling bandits often reduce to online learning?
questions.choice_A: By converting pairwise feedback into multiclass labels for each context
questions.choice_B: By forming an adversarial zero-sum game over policies and applying no-regret learning (e.g., Sparring or Exp4-style methods)
questions.choice_C: By replacing pairwise outcomes with estimated utilities
questions.choice_D: By ignoring contexts to increase sample efficiency

questions.question: Which statement about sample complexity in offline preference learning is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: Uniformly sampling all pairs is always optimal for learning
questions.choice_B: Learning over a large policy class requires a number of labeled pairs scaling with its capacity (e.g., VC/Natarajan/Rademacher complexity)
questions.choice_C: Pairwise labels provide strictly less information than pointwise labels for generalization
questions.choice_D: Sample complexity is independent of noise in pairwise comparisons

questions.question: What is a key difference between strong regret and weak regret in dueling bandits?
questions.choice_A: Strong regret compares against the best mixed strategy; weak regret compares against the worst arm
questions.choice_B: Strong regret requires at least one of the played arms to be optimal; weak regret requires both
questions.choice_C: Strong regret penalizes rounds where neither chosen arm is the best, while weak regret does not penalize if at least one chosen arm is optimal
questions.choice_D: There is no difference; the terms are synonymous

questions.question: Why can focusing on the Borda winner be suboptimal in the presence of preference cycles?
questions.choice_A: The Borda winner is undefined without utility normalization
questions.choice_B: The Borda score ignores the variance of pairwise outcomes
questions.choice_C: The Borda winner may perform poorly in head-to-head matchups even with a high average score
questions.choice_D: The Borda winner is always dominated by the Condorcet winner

questions.question: In the game-theoretic formulation of dueling bandits, what do the rows and columns of the payoff matrix represent?
questions.choice_A: Rows are contexts; columns are losses
questions.choice_B: Rows and columns are arms (or policies), and entries are expected pairwise win probabilities minus 1/2
questions.choice_C: Rows are features; columns are labels
questions.choice_D: Rows are time steps; columns are rewards

questions.question: Which challenge is specific to contextual preference learning compared to non-contextual dueling bandits?
questions.choice_A: Estimating absolute utilities for each arm
questions.choice_B: Handling preference cycles in the pairwise matrix
questions.choice_C: Generalizing across contexts with sparse pairwise comparisons per context
questions.choice_D: Ensuring the Condorcet winner exists

questions.question: What is a practical benefit of algorithms that target the von Neumann winner in high-noise environments?
questions.choice_A: They can exactly identify a single best arm with fewer comparisons
questions.choice_B: They remain well-defined and robust when no deterministic ranking exists
questions.choice_C: They never need exploration
questions.choice_D: They guarantee linear time complexity regardless of the number of arms

questions.question: Which statement best captures the aim of Dueling Bandit Gradient Descent (DBGD) in learning to rank?
questions.choice_A: Estimate absolute relevance labels from clicks
questions.choice_B: Use interleaved comparisons to perform stochastic gradient steps guided by preference feedback
questions.choice_C: Eliminate documents with low empirical mean reward
questions.choice_D: Perform exhaustive pairwise comparisons among all documents

questions.question: In offline-to-online guarantees for contextual preference learning, which condition is typically required for reliable counterfactual evaluation?
questions.choice_A: The logging policy must be deterministic
questions.choice_B: Positivity/overlap: logged data must have nonzero probability for the policy’s chosen comparisons
questions.choice_C: The contexts must be i.i.d. Gaussian
questions.choice_D: There must be a Condorcet winner in every context

questions.question: What is a common regret rate for algorithms in stochastic dueling bandits under standard assumptions (e.g., BTL with gaps)?
questions.choice_A: Regret grows linearly in time
questions.choice_B: Regret is constant after a burn-in period
questions.choice_C: Regret scales as O(log T) up to problem-dependent constants
questions.choice_D: Regret scales as O(T^{1/2} log T) universally

questions.question: Why might elimination-based dueling algorithms need careful tie-handling?
questions.choice_A: Ties imply that the stochastic model is misspecified
questions.choice_B: Ties can cause cyclic elimination unless confidence intervals account for near-equality
questions.choice_C: Ties force the algorithm to switch to absolute reward estimation
questions.choice_D: Ties guarantee the existence of a Condorcet winner

questions.question: When comparing online and offline preference learning, which statement is most accurate regarding sample efficiency?
questions.choice_A: Offline learning is always less sample-efficient because exploration is impossible
questions.choice_B: Online learning can target informative comparisons adaptively, often reducing sample complexity compared to passively collected offline data
questions.choice_C: Offline learning requires no assumptions about logging policies for valid evaluation
questions.choice_D: Online and offline learning have identical sample complexity if the model is well-specified
